readerTitle: Different prices for the same thing: when it works and when it backfires
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Amazon, 2000년 DVD 가격 테스트) + 가상 사례 (청소 서비스, IT 지원 회사)
insight: 가격 차별은 판매자가 몰래 고객을 추측할 때 실패하고, 고객이 눈에 보이는 울타리(시간, 자격, 약정, 수량) 중 한쪽을 스스로 고를 때 성공한다.
misconception: 고객마다 다른 가격은 원래 불공정하다. 또는 반대로, 고객이 낼 수 있는 만큼 알아내서 받기만 하면 된다.

sources.text: Amazon statement and press coverage on its DVD price test, September 2000 (e.g., Washington Post, Bloomberg, Wall Street Journal reports)
경제학 표준 개념 (가격 차별, 지불 의사, 자기 선택 방식의 가격 울타리)
청소 서비스와 IT 지원 회사 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Amazon DVD 가격 테스트: 2000년 9월 DVD 팬 포럼(DVD Talk) 사용자들이 같은 DVD의 가격이 사람마다 다르다는 것을 발견. Amazon은 무작위 가격 테스트였고 고객 데이터 기반이 아니었다고 밝히며 사과하고, 더 많이 낸 고객에게 차액을 환불했다고 보도됨. 날짜, 포럼 이름, 환불 방식은 게시 전에 1차 보도로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 환불 인원·금액 수치를 넣지 않았습니다.
가상 수치 확인: 청소 $120 기본가, 토요일 할증과 정기 계약 할인은 설명용. IT 지원 시간당 $150, 비영리 요율 $110은 가상 수치입니다.
주의 카드의 법률 문구는 특정 국가 법률 조언이 아니라 일반적 언급(많은 지역에서 인종·성별 등 개인 특성에 따른 가격 차별 제한)으로만 썼습니다. 표현이 과하지 않은지 검토하세요.

cards.title: Same DVD, same day, different price
body: In September 2000, shoppers on a DVD fan forum noticed something odd. The same movie on Amazon seemed to cost different amounts for different people.
Amazon called it a short price test. Customers called it unfair. The idea behind it is one of the most useful in pricing. The way it was done is a lesson in how not to use it.

image.label: Two shoppers seeing different prices for the same DVD
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 두 사람이 나란히 노트북 화면을 보고 있고, 같은 DVD 표지 옆에 서로 다른 가격표가 떠 있음. 한 사람은 눈살을 찌푸림. 실제 로고나 영화 제목은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Some clients would happily pay more.
body: You run a house-cleaning business. A standard clean is $120.
You suspect owners of big houses on wealthy streets would pay $150 without blinking. Meanwhile, some retired clients can barely manage $120. How do you price?

options.text: Quote each client privately, higher for homes that look wealthy
options.feedback: You may capture more money at first. But neighbors talk, and clients who learn they paid more for the same clean feel cheated and leave.

options.text: Keep one price of $120 for everyone
options.feedback: Simple and fair-looking. But you leave money on the table from clients who'd pay more, and still lose those who can't pay $120.

options.text: Publish clear options: a Saturday premium, a discount for regular weekday bookings, a seniors' rate
options.feedback: Clients pick their own price by choosing a time, a commitment or a group they qualify for. Nobody is guessed at, so nobody feels tricked.

cards.title: The problem wasn't different prices. It was secret ones.
body: Forum members compared notes and felt tricked. The story spread fast in the press.
Within weeks, Amazon apologized. It said the prices had been random, not based on who was shopping, and refunded the difference to buyers who had paid more.
Notice what customers didn't object to. Nobody complains that a movie matinee costs less than an evening show. The anger came from hidden prices with no reason anyone could see.

cards.title: Price discrimination
body: **Price discrimination** means charging different customers different prices for the same thing, because they value it differently, not because it costs you more to serve them.
One price misses twice. Some customers would have paid more. Others would have bought only at a lower price. Different prices let you reach both.

image.label: One price line missing high and low payers
image.brief: 가로로 늘어선 사람 아이콘들, 머리 위에 각자 낼 의향이 있는 금액. 가운데 하나의 가격선이 지나감. 선 위쪽 사람들 옆에는 "Would pay more", 선 아래쪽에는 "Walks away" 라벨.

cards.title: Build fences customers choose for themselves.
body: The trick is a **fence**: a visible rule that separates prices, which customers sort themselves across.
list: **Time:** off-peak, weekday or early booking costs less
**Quantity:** lower price per unit for bigger orders
**Effort:** coupons for those willing to clip them
cards.callout: The seller sets the fence. The customer decides which side to stand on.
cards.softwareNote: Student plans, startup programs and discounts for paying a year upfront are all fences. Each one lowers the price for customers who value the product less, without cutting it for everyone else.

cards.title: A fence only works if it holds.
body: If anyone can claim the seniors' rate or the nonprofit price, it quietly becomes your real price. Check eligibility, or tie the cheaper price to a real condition, like a weekday slot.
The reason must also feel fair. A discount for students reads as kind. A surcharge for people who look rich reads as a trap.
And some fences are off limits. Many places restrict pricing by personal traits such as race or gender. Check the rules where you operate.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support firm.
body: You provide IT support to offices at $150 an hour. Large law firms pay without fuss. Small nonprofits keep turning you down as too expensive, and you have spare hours midweek.

options.text: Quietly quote big firms $190 and nonprofits $120, based on how they look
options.feedback: More revenue on paper. But clients share vendors and compare invoices, and an unexplained gap can cost you your best accounts.

options.text: Offer a published nonprofit rate of $110, with proof of status and midweek scheduling
options.feedback: You fill idle hours with new clients, and the fence keeps law firms at $150. The cost is checking eligibility and holding the scheduling rule.

options.text: Cut the price to $120 for everyone
options.feedback: You'd win the nonprofits, but every law firm that happily paid $150 now pays $30 less an hour for the same work.

cards.title: Different prices work when customers choose them.
body: Charging customers differently can be fair and profitable, as long as the difference rests on a visible fence, not a secret guess.
**Try it today:** list the customers who say no to your price. Is there a time, group or commitment fence that could reach them without lowering the price for everyone else?
